line:
I sit up slowly and bow my head over Cal Tarn, laying my hand on the coat that covers him. "Cal, you ran those hares since you were nine, and you came because you were asked. I'll carry your name back to the Widow, and to Tam, and I won't forget it."

Then I turn to Hob. "Thank you for the light, and there's nothing to forgive. Will the lamp hold until dawn without you, and do the hungry ones know of any other way up from under the stones? I need to get back to Wil by first light, and I'd like to bring Cal home to his people rather than leave him here."

entries.text:
Hob bows his head to the coat, and the dull coins of his eyes seem to soften. "Cal Tarn," he says, as if learning the name. "I will keep it... with the others I could not keep."

He turns his face up to the lamp. "It burns... while there is oil, and while I tend it. There is a pony's worth of oil in the packs, and a full cask in the cellar-niche behind the plinth. Enough until the moon turns. But I cannot leave it. I am... of it now." He is quiet a moment. "The hungry ones came up through one stone, the one they dragged aside. The floor is old, and the cellar below is older. I do not know every way under. Only that the light has kept them from this one door." The flame steadies, and he adds, "They are patient. Two roam. One is wounded. Hunger makes them bold, and the light does not reach the village."

Your body answers the question for you. You have 1 HP, a bruised and aching chest, and no prayers left in you. The lamp-house floor is warm with its glow, and the clearing is quiet. Cal lies heavy and still under his coat. You could carry or drag him a mile down the track, but not quickly, and not safely, in the state you're in.

It is just before midnight, and dawn is six or seven hours off. You can rest here under the lamp, where the ghouls will not come near, or you can set out now with Cal and your wounds, and reach Hollow Reach well before first light, but weak and without your prayers.

entries.text:
The scene is set and the tool calls above went through. The clock now reads Day 2, 12:05 AM, and the notebook has Hob's new details.

Brannoc is at 1 HP with no spell slots, and he has about six hours before dawn. You can rest under the lamp's light, or rig a litter and carry Cal home. What does Brannoc do?

You kneel by Cal and lay your hand on the coat, and the hymn comes unbidden, low and cracked. Hob waits until you finish. Then he rises, joints creaking like old harness, and looks up at the lamp.

"Burns... till dawn. Oil enough." He nods toward the burst saddlebags, where two flasks lie unbroken in the straw. "I must stay. The flame is mine to keep. If I leave it, it dies, and they come." His head turns toward the black gap behind the lamp-house door, where the flagstone lies shut. "One way up. The stone. But the two that roam... they will come home before sunrise. Hungry ones always return to the dark by day. They will find the light between them and their hole. I cannot say what they will do."

He pauses, and his dry voice softens. "Wil's wound is not... the poison it looks. I smelled it on the wind. Not rot. Only fever. Clean it, keep it cool, he will mend. You have time. Not much."

That leaves your choices. You are at 1 HP, with no spells, and a mile of dark track down to the village. The pony's gear has a stout canvas tarp and two straps, enough to rig a drag-litter for Cal, though hauling a grown man downhill alone will be hard going in your state. The light of the lamp is the only safe ground within a mile. If you rest here under it, you could get a short rest in the next hour, and a few spells more by morning, but Wil would wait.

entries.text:
The house at the lane's far end is small and neat, with a swept step and a hare-skin drying on a peg by the door. You knock softly and wait. The door opens on a narrow, upright woman of fifty or so with Cal's quick eyes. She looks at the bow in your hands before she looks at you, and she already knows.

"Come in," she says. "Sit."

You sit at her table, and she does not cry yet. You tell it plainly, as you promised yourself: that Cal knew the track since he was nine, that he went up in the dark because you asked and never turned back, that he loosed arrow after arrow with his own life ebbing, and that it was his shots that brought down the first of them and kept you alive. You tell her Hob lit the Lamp, and that Cal lay under it in his own coat, in its light, until his neighbors came for him. You hold out the bow in both hands.

She takes it and holds it a long while against her chest. Then the tears come, quietly, and you hum Edda's hymn low until she lets you. When she can speak, she says only, "He liked being asked." After a moment she adds, "Put his name on the Lamp. I'll send his lantern up every week, the old brass one. It was his father's."

She presses a small loaf of bread and a wedge of hard cheese on you before you go, and will not hear no. You also tell her you will carry word of Hob to his sister, and she nods. "Maud Marrow. Greywater, past the mill. Tell her Hob kept his lamp." The bread and cheese are for the road.

It is half past ten. Your prayers are all ready, the powder is in your pack, and the Lamp's rota is set. Greywater is a day's walk down the valley, and the road beyond is open. The Reach has already begun to lift its head, and Tam is watching you from the lane, waiting to see what you do.

Then she takes the bow, runs her thumb along the worn grip, and says only, "He oiled this every Sunday." Her eyes are dry, and then they aren't, and you stay as long as she needs, humming low, until the kettle goes cold.

When she is steadier she says, "Put his name on the rota. No. I'll carry the oil myself, in his name, once a week. It's a walk he made a hundred times." She looks at you. "And you tell Hob's sister. Somebody should. Tell her he kept the light." The bow is hers now, and it is off your sheet.

It is half past ten. You have the powder, a rota that has taken root, Greywater a day down the valley, and a village at your back. The Lamp still needs its first shift, Hob should hear the plan, and the sealed slab sits quiet in its ring of lamps.

The house at the lane's end is small and swept clean, with a withered bunch of last year's yarrow hung by the door. You knock softly and wait. The door opens after a long moment on a small, upright woman with Cal's quick dark eyes, and they are red-rimmed but dry. She looks at your amulet, then at the bow in your hands, and steps back without a word to let you in.

You sit with her at a scrubbed table. You tell her all of it: how he knew every bend of the north track, how he went because he was asked, how he held the light steady and loosed arrow after arrow with the ghouls on top of him, and how he never once turned back. You do not hurry, and you hum when your voice fails. When you finish, she is quiet for a long while. Then she takes the bow from you in both hands, as you held it, and lays it across her knees like something that might wake.

"He ran hares up there since he was nine," she says at last. "I told him it was a lonely track." She breathes in, once. "He wasn't lonely at the end, was he? You were there."

"I was there," you say. It is close enough to true that you let it stand.

She nods. She asks that his name be carved on the lintel of the Lamp, where travellers can read it, and says she will carry oil up the north track herself on the first of every month, for as long as she has legs. She asks nothing about the rota beyond that, but her hand rests a moment on yours when you rise, dry and light as paper. At the door she says, "Tell Hob's sister, when you find her. Tell her the keeper was kept." You will remember that.

It is eleven in the morning on Day 3. The bow is home. You have all three slots, a pouch of silver-and-iron powder, and a message to carry down the valley to Greywater, a day's walk away, to a weaver named Maud Marrow. Hob keeps the Lamp, the rota is forming, and the ghouls lie silent under the stones. The road goes on from the far side of the Reach.

entries.text:
The house at the end of the lane is small and neat, with a wreath of dried herbs on the door and the shutters closed. You knock softly and wait. After a long moment the door opens a hand's width, and a thin woman with Cal's grey eyes looks at you and at what you carry in both hands.

She doesn't speak. She opens the door and steps back.

You sit at her table, and the hearth is cold because no one has had the heart to light it. You tell her everything, plainly and gently. Cal knew the track since he was nine. He went because he was asked and because he was the best man for it. He never once turned back, and it was his arrow that dropped the first ghoul. He did not die alone, Hob was beside him, and he lay under the lamp's light afterward with his coat around him until his own people came. You hum a few bars of Edda's hymn when your voice falters, and she lets you.

When you're done, she takes the bow from you in both hands, as you held it out, and runs her thumb along the grip where it is worn smooth. She is quiet a long time.

"He'd have wanted to go that way," she says at last, in a voice like dry paper. "Not young. But useful." Then: "Put his name on the rota. And when the Lamp has a door, I'd have the bow hang beside it, where a traveller can see it." She looks up, and her eyes are bright and steady. "Tell Hob Marrow he's no keeper of one. He's the keeper of two."

She makes you tea on a fire she lights herself. You stay until noon, and when you leave she walks you to her gate, which she has not done for anyone in four days.

You've now carried Cal home and set the Lamp's rota in motion. It is almost 11 in the morning on Day 3, and you have all three prayers, Channel Divinity, a pouch of powder, and the whole day. Greywater is a day's walk down the valley, and Maud Marrow doesn't know her brother is dead. Wil is on the mend, the Reach is quiet, and the barrow is sealed.

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~9-12: Brannoc told Maud of Hob's death and gave her the blue shawl and Hob's words. Maud is a broad-shouldered, grey-haired weaver in her sixties with ink-blue fingers; she talks a lot, as Hob said. She wept, then insisted on coming to see the Lamp and bring dyed wool and oil. She offered Brannoc a night's lodging and a loom-house meal.

entries.text:
The girl points with her chin and hurries off with her basket. You swing the shield onto your back and walk down between the drying racks, wool in red and blue and ochre moving gently in the wind, to the house by the weir. The blue door is old and faded to the color of a winter sky. You knock twice, softly.

Maud Marrow opens it with a shuttle still in her hand. She is a broad, gray-haired woman in her sixties, with her sleeves pushed up and dye stained blue into every crease of her fingers. She takes in the amulet, then your face, and the shuttle slowly lowers. "You're from the Reach," she says. "Or from Hob." You say you are from Hob. Her mouth tightens, and she steps aside.

You sit at her table beside the loom, with the weir loud outside. You tell it all in your own words, as you promised: that he kept the light, that he did not leave it, that when the dark came he stood between it and the village in the only way left to him. You do not hide what he had become. She listens with her hands flat on the table, and does not interrupt, which is the only way you know she is a woman who talks. When you reach his words, you give them exactly, and then you take the blue shawl from your pack and lay it in her lap.

She presses it to her face. For a long time the only sound is the weir. Then she laughs, a wet, startled sound. "'Had somewhere to be.' He would. Forty years of that man having somewhere to be." She wipes her eyes with the corner of the wool. "It was warm, he said? Every night?" You say that was what he asked you to tell her, and she nods and keeps nodding.

By noon she has fed you bread, cheese, and a bowl of sharp pickled beets, and has decided, in a flurry of wool and orders, that she is going to the Lamp herself. She'll bring dyed fleeces for the rota, and oil, and sit a night or two on the step beside him, "since the stubborn old fool never would come home." She presses a coil of dyed yarn into your hand as thanks, a deep, steady blue.

With that, the word is carried. The Lamp has its keepers, the rota is set, and the Reach has its lanterns lit. It is noon on Day 4. You have 300 XP and will need 900 for level 3, and Lesser Restoration is waiting for you there. You have a village behind you that will remember your name, and a road ahead that you don't yet know.

The girl points without a word, then trots ahead of you to the lower end of the village. The house with the blue door is narrow and tall, with a loom's clack coming through the shutters. It stops when you knock.

Maud Marrow is a brisk, grey-haired woman near sixty, with her brother's heavy brows and wool-stained hands. She looks at you, the amulet, the shield on your back, and the careful way you stand. She knows before you speak. "He's dead, then," she says, flatly, and steps back to let you in.

You sit by her loom and tell it in your own words: the Lamp gone dark, the hungry ones, how he came to a barn door to beg for light, how he kept it burning afterward, and that the lamp-house is lit tonight because of him. You give her his words one by one, carefully. When you reach the shawl, you take it from your pack and lay it across her knees. She holds it a long time, and she cries without noise, the way people do who have wept alone before. Then you say, "He said you would tell him he should have come home. He said to tell you he had somewhere to be." Maud laughs, a short, wet bark. "Stubborn old goat," she says. "I knew it. I knew he'd never come down off that hill."

She feeds you bread and hot tea, and does not let you leave before noon. She says she will come to the Lamp with the next cart and sit a night with him, and she presses a bolt of undyed wool cloth on you for the road, which you can carry or sell. She also tells you, quietly, that Greywater has no healer and no priest, and its chapel has stood shut since the last one died. There are always coughs, she says, and a child with a bad foot.

You have kept your promise to Hob, and you have earned 100 XP for it. That brings you to 400 of the 900 you need for level 3. Lamp Watch is done. Maud's bolt of cloth is yours if you want it, and the road goes on.

input.add_to_description: Day 4 ~9–12: Brannoc told her of Hob's death and gave her the blue shawl and his message. Maud is a lean, sharp-tongued woman of about sixty with ink-blue fingertips. She grieved, scolded, laughed, and decided to visit the Lamp herself; she offered to weave wicks and a banner for the lamp-house and to send a cart of oil from Greywater.
Day 4 ~noon: Maud Marrow told. She will travel to the Lamp within the week and arrange Greywater oil. Quest essentially complete.

entries.text: sheet: lost 1 × Blue shawl (Maud Marrow's, to return to her); XP +100: 400

The girl points without a word, then runs ahead of you down the lane, basket bumping on her hip. By the time you reach the blue door, the news that a stranger is asking after the weaver's brother has gone ahead of you. You unsling your shield and hang it on your back. You knock, softly.

The door opens on a lean, sharp-faced woman of about sixty, with ink-blue fingertips and her gray hair bound in a scarf. She looks at your amulet, and at your face, and her mouth goes tight before you have said a word. "He's dead, isn't he," she says. "Come in, then."

You say it the way you planned. You tell her your name, that you come from Hob, and that you have something of hers. You sit at her table, with the loom ticking cold in the next room, and you tell her all of it. You tell her about the dark lamp, the ghouls under the stones, and the night Hob came to the barn door begging for light, and that he kept the Lamp lit to the end. You hand her the shawl. She holds it against her face a long moment. Then you give her his words, exactly as he said them: that he kept the light, that he was not afraid, that it was warm every night, that she would say he should have come home, and that he had somewhere to be.

She laughs, a short cracked sound, and then she is crying, and she is still scolding him through it. "Somewhere to be. Forty years of somewhere to be." She wipes her face with the shawl and then, to your surprise, folds it carefully over her knee. "He was always the stubborn one. I told him that lamp would be the death of him." She is quiet. "I'm glad it wasn't for nothing."

By noon she has made tea, fed you bread and soft cheese, and decided what she will do. She will walk up to the Lamp herself within the week, whatever the road, and see him. She will weave good wicks for the lamp-house and a banner for the door, and send a cart of Greywater oil, so the Reach need not carry it all. She presses two silver pieces and a hand-dyed scarf the blue of her shawl into your hand. You hold out the coin to refuse, but she is already shaking her head. "Take it. He'd have wanted you fed."

You've seen the message through. That is 100 XP for it, and you are at 400 of the 900 you need for level 3. It is just after noon, and you stand at Maud's door with a full belly, full prayers, and no one left in the road ahead of you to carry anything to. The valley is bright and open. The chapel in Greywater has no priest, and the sick, if any, are for you to find.

The girl with the basket points without a word, and then she hurries ahead of you, because in a village this size news runs faster than a man walks. By the time you reach the house with the blue door, it is already open.

"You said Hob," she says.

You ask to come in, and she steps aside. Her loom stands in the front room, half a green length on it, and she sits down on the bench before it as if her knees have decided for her. You give her your name and where you've come from. You tell her in your own words, slowly: the dark lamp, the thing at the barn door that begged for light, the keeper who rose to ask for help for the sake of strangers and stayed to see the fire lit. You say that he is dead, and has been since harvest, and that he is bound to the Lamp's light now, and that he is not in pain.

She doesn't interrupt. Her hands twist in her apron, and the flour makes pale marks in the cloth.

Then you take out the blue shawl and set it in her lap. She stares at it. Her thumb finds a dropped stitch near the hem. "I never did mend that," she whispers, and for the first time her face breaks.

You give her his words in his order: that he kept the light, that he was not afraid at the end, that the shawl was warm every night. At the last, you say that she will tell him he should have come home, and that he said to tell her he had somewhere to be. She laughs, a wet, cracked sound, and says, "Of course I would. The stubborn old fool." Then she weeps in earnest, and you sit by her and hum low until it eases.

An hour passes, then two. Maud makes tea no one drinks. She asks a hundred questions, and you answer every one. By the time the sun is full over the weir, she has made up her mind. She will see him. She will walk to the Lamp herself, or ride with the first carter going north, and she will sit with him at the step. And she insists, with a flash of the old sharpness, on sending a bolt of her best cloth back with you for the families in the Reach who have lost their men.

You have 100 XP for finishing what you promised, for 400 total, 500 short of level 3. Your pack feels lighter. It is a little past nine, and the weaver is steadier than she was. You have a road, a free morning, a village with a shut chapel and no priest, and prayers still full.

Sixtyish, brisk, grey braid, talkative, fierce; she had not heard from Hob since harvest and feared the worst. Brannoc told her of his death, his message and gave her the blue shawl.

entries.text:
The girl with the yarn basket points without a word, then follows you with her eyes. The lane runs down between racks of dyed wool, red and blue and ochre, steaming faintly in the pale sun, to the weir at the bottom. The blue door is open a hand's breadth, and a steady clack-and-thump comes from inside, the sound of a loom.

You slide the shield onto your back and knock. The loom stops mid-throw.

Maud Marrow is a lean woman in her sixties, with a long gray braid over one shoulder and wool lint in her hair. She looks at your amulet, your mail, your face, and her eyes go very still before you speak. You say what you meant to: your name, that you come from Hob, that you have something of hers in your pack and would tell her about him in your own words.

"He's dead," she says. It is not a question. "I knew it at harvest. The lamp went dark, and he'd never have let it." Her mouth works. "Come in, then. Sit. Don't stand on my step like a bailiff."

Her loom-house is warm and bright, with skeins hung from every beam and a kettle on the hob. You sit on a stool by the cold fire and tell it all, as plainly as you told Nessa: the ghouls under the stones, the lamp put out, how Hob came begging at the barn door in the dark, how he lit the lamp again with his own hands and held the dead at bay through the night. You give her his words exactly: that he kept the light, that he was not afraid at the end, that the shawl was warm every night, and that he had somewhere to be.

When you draw the blue shawl from your pack and lay it across her knees, she doesn't speak. She smooths it with one hand, and her thumb finds a place near the hem where the weave is uneven. "My first try at that pattern," she says. "He wore it anyway." Then she laughs, a short, cracked sound, and wipes her face on her sleeve. "'I had somewhere to be.' Stubborn old goat. Forty years on a hill with a lamp, and he still gets the last word."

She is quiet a while. Then she looks up, brisk again, though her eyes are red. "You'll eat. Don't argue. And then I want to know about this rota of yours, and who is carrying oil, and when I can go up that hill and sit with my brother. I'll not have him tended by strangers alone."

It is twenty past nine in the morning. Maud has a kettle on, a loom-house full of questions, and the first real welcome you have had in days. Hollow Reach is a day behind you, the Lamp is lit, and the village is safe. What does Brannoc do?

The girl with the yarn basket points without a word. Her face has already read something in yours. Down by the weir, at the lower end of the village, the house with the blue door stands against the white noise of the water. You sling your shield on your back, as you said, and knock softly.

The door opens on a sturdy woman of about sixty, with a weaver's forearms, ink-blue fingers, and Hob's long jaw. She has a bobbin in one hand. She takes in the amulet, then your face, and the bobbin goes still.

"Maud Marrow? My name is Brannoc, and I come from Hob. May I come in? I have something of yours in my pack, and I'd like to tell you about him in my own words."

She stands there a moment too long. Then she steps back. "Sit," she says. "I'll not have it said on a doorstep."

You tell her, in the house with the loom and the smell of wool and woad, with the weir roaring outside. You tell it as Hob would have wanted: that he kept the light to the end, that he was not afraid, that he asked for her to be told the shawl was warm every night. You give her the shawl last, folded the way you carried it. She holds it in both hands and puts her face into it, and for a time she says nothing at all.

When she speaks, it is fast and a little too bright, the way people talk to hold something down. "I told him to come home. Every winter, I told him. He never would. Never one for company, only lamps." She laughs once, a wet sound. "I had a letter written. It's on the loom-bench. I was waiting for a carter." Then she is quiet again, and says, "I'll go up. I'll sit with him a night. If he'll know me." You tell her he will. You tell her what he said last, that he had somewhere to be, and she nods slowly and says, "That sounds like Hob."

She presses a small bundle on you when you leave: a pair of wool gloves, plain gray, that she says were meant for a brother who would not have worn them. You take them, and you add 100 XP for a hard errand done well, putting you at 400 of the 900 needed for level 3.

It is nine in the morning on Day 4. The village is bright and busy, with the dye racks steaming. The chapel at the near end has no priest, and you may notice the people looking at you. The three ghouls still wait below the slab, and Hollow Reach is two days behind you. You have your prayers, full health, and a road in front of you.

What does Brannoc do?

Her hands do not stop moving, smoothing the same fold of her apron over and over. When you reach "I kept the light, and I wasn't afraid," her mouth presses thin. When you give her the shawl, soft, blue, faded, smelling of lamp oil, she pulls it against her face and her shoulders shake.

Then you say the last line, the way he said it: "She talks too much. She will say I should have come home. Tell her I had somewhere to be." And she laughs, a wet, startled laugh that turns into another thing. "That old goat," she says. "That stubborn old goat. He did, too. Somewhere to be." She wipes her face with the shawl. "Forty years I said he should come home. Forty years."

She asks you everything: the Lamp, the ghouls, the village, Cal, the oil. She makes you eat, though you have already breakfasted. By midday she has decided. She will go up to Hollow Reach with the next carter heading that way, in two days, and sit with him at the Lamp, and stay on the rota as long as her legs will carry her. "Somebody ought to bring the old fool a shawl in winter," she says. "Properly. And hear what the dead have to say, if they'll say it."

I nod to the girl and ask gently, "Good morning. Could you tell me where Maud Marrow the weaver lives? I've come with word of her brother."

Then I walk down to the house with the blue door, shield slung on my back so I look less like a soldier, and knock. When she opens, I'll say, "Maud Marrow? My name is Brannoc, and I come from Hob. The girl with the yarn basket points without a word. Her eyes go to your amulet, then to the blue door at the lower end by the weir. You walk down between the racks of dyed wool, the shield slung on your back, and knock.

The door opens on a sturdy woman of sixty or so with a grey braid down her back and dye-stained fingers. Behind her the loom stands half-warped, and the room smells of lanolin and woodsmoke. Her eyes go over you quickly: young, tired, a cleric's amulet. "Healer, is it? I've no sick here." Then you say your name and Hob's, and her face changes.

You tell her in your own words, sitting at her kitchen table with a cup of her tea going cold. You tell her he is dead, and was dead when you met him, and that the death was an old one; he had been keeping the light for weeks beyond it. You tell her about the lamp, the ghouls, what he did to hold them down, and that he spoke at the end of her. You give her his words as he gave them: that he kept the light, that he was not afraid, that the shawl was warm every night. Then you lift the blue shawl from your pack and lay it across her hands.

She does not cry at first. She holds the shawl to her face and breathes in the lamp-smoke on it. Then she makes a sound that is half a sob and half a laugh. "Had somewhere to be," she says. "The stubborn old goat. Forty years on a hill talking to nobody, and he had somewhere to be." She wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist. "I told him to come home. Every harvest, I told him. Gods, I talk too much." And she laughs again, wetly, and you laugh with her, because it is exactly what Hob said she would say.

She makes you eat bread and honey, and she will not hear of payment. Before you go she presses a folded scarf into your hands, blue wool in her own close weave, with a small red thread knotted in one corner. "For the road," she says. "A cleric ought to be warm." She will walk up to the Lamp herself next week, she says, with her own oil, and sit with him a while.

It is half past nine on Day 4. You have 350 of 900 XP toward the next level, full hit points, and all your prayers. The valley road runs on past Greywater to wherever you choose to take it. Hollow Reach is a day behind you, the Lamp is lit, and the rest of the world is ahead.
